summary.text: 开 means “open” and “begin.” It is the standardized simplified form of 開. The older graph’s construction is disputed: the familiar account of hands opening a latched door is not established as its original formation.

formation.text: 开 is derived from 開 through standard simplification. Historical analyses differ over whether 開 combines 門 and 幵 as meaningful elements or uses 幵 for its sound. The popular hands-and-latch explanation remains an interpretation, not a settled account of the graph’s origin.

history.text: The 1956 simplification scheme pairs 开 with 開. The simplified graph omits 門; this graphic change does not resolve the competing analyses of the older graph.

uncertainties.text: The received Shuowen analysis treats 門 and 幵 as components, while Duan Yucai treats 幵 as phonetic. A separate paleographic argument proposes that 幵 was an earlier graph used for the word 開. These proposals leave the older graph’s construction unsettled.

senses.text: 开 means “open”; its earliest occurrence is not dated here.
开 also means “begin,” “initiate,” or “start.” Its chronological relation to “open” is unresolved.
The received Shuowen entry glosses 開 as “stretch/open.” This is a historical dictionary interpretation, not a dated first meaning.
A paleographic argument proposes these as early uses of 開 and suggests 啟 was more commonly used for opening doors. This proposal does not establish a settled chronology.

limitations.text: No dated progression among “stretch/open,” “open,” “begin,” or the proposed instructing, explaining, and releasing senses is established, so no semantic development is asserted.

overview.text: 开 means “open” and can also mean “begin.” It is the standardized simplified form of 開. The familiar explanation of hands opening a latched door is not established as the older graph’s origin.

relationships.text: 开 is the standardized simplified counterpart of 開, explicitly paired with it in the 1956 simplification scheme; the simplified graph omits 門.
